danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 9
paragraphs: Det var aftenen før Skt. Nikolaj-dagen, den femte december 1820. Natasja havde boet hos sin bror med sin mand og børn siden det tidlige efterår. Pierre var taget til Petersborg i sine egne ærinder for tre uger, som han sagde, men var blevet der næsten syv uger og ventedes hjem hvert øjeblik.
Foruden Bezukhov-familien (Pierres familie) boede også Nikolajs gamle ven, den pensionerede general Vasilij Dmitritsj Denisov, hos Rostov-familien denne femte december.

Nikolaj vidste, at den sjette, på hans navnedag, ville huset være fuldt af gæster. Da måtte han bytte sin tatariske kjortel ud med kjolefrakken, trække i snævre, spidssnudede støvler og køre hen til den nye kirke, han havde bygget. Bagefter måtte han tage imod gratulanterne, byde på noget at spise og drikke og tale om valgene til adelens tillidsposter. Men aftenen før mente han at have ret til at tilbringe som sædvanlig. Han gennemgik forvalterens regnskaber for den landsby i Rjazan, der tilhørte hans kones nevø, skrev to forretningsbreve og så til kornmagasinerne, kvæggårdene og staldene inden middagen. Da han havde truffet sine forholdsregler mod den almindelige fuldskab, man kunne vente sig næste dag, fordi det var en stor helgendag, vendte han hjem til middagen. Uden at have haft et øjeblik alene med sin kone satte han sig ved det lange bord med tyve kuverter, hvor hele husstanden var samlet. Der sad hans mor, hendes gamle selskabsdame Belova, hans kone, deres tre børn med guvernante og huslærer, hans kones nevø med sin huslærer, Sonja, Denisov, Natasja og hendes tre børn og deres guvernante, og den gamle Mikhail Ivanovitj, den afdøde fyrstes arkitekt, som levede sine sidste år på godset.

Grevinde Marja sad for den anden bordende. Da hendes mand satte sig, sluttede hun — af den hurtige måde, hvorpå han efter at have taget sin serviet skubbede det glas og vinglas, der stod foran ham, til side — at han var i dårligt humør, som det sommetider var tilfældet, når han kom til middag direkte fra forretningerne, især når han lige havde forladt forvalteren. Grevinde Marja vidste udmærket godt, hvad det humør var, og når hun selv var i godt humør, ventede hun roligt, til han havde fået de første retter, og forsøgte først da at tale til ham og få ham til at indrømme, at han var i dårligt humør uden grund; men i dag glemte hun helt den forsigtighedsregel; hun var bedrøvet og såret over, at han var i dårligt humør med hende, og følte sig ulykkelig. Hun spurgte ham, hvor han havde været. Han svarede. Hun spurgte igen, om godsets sager gik godt. Han rynkede panden ubehageligt og svarede kort.

»Så tog jeg ikke fejl,« tænkte grevinde Marja. »Hvorfor er han vred på mig?« Hun sluttede af hans tone, at han var irriteret på hende og ønskede at afslutte samtalen. Hun vidste, at hendes bemærkninger lød unaturlige, men kunne ikke lade være med at stille et par spørgsmål til.

Takket være Denisov blev samtalen ved bordet snart livlig og almindelig, og hun talte ikke til sin mand. Da de forlod bordet og som sædvanlig gik ind for at takke den gamle grevinde, rakte grevinde Marja hånden frem og kyssede sin mand og spurgte ham, hvorfor han var vred på hende.
»Du har altid sådanne mærkværdige indfald! Jeg tænkte slet ikke på at være vred,« svarede han.
Men ordet altid syntes hende at indebære: »Jo, jeg er vred, men jeg vil ikke sige dig hvorfor.«

Nikolaj og hans kone levede så lykkeligt sammen, at selv Sonja og den gamle grevinde, der følte sig skinsyge og gerne ville have set dem uenige, ikke kunne finde noget at bebrejde dem; men selv de havde deres øjeblikke af fjendtlighed. Af og til — og det var altid lige efter at de havde været allerlykkeligst sammen — blev de pludselig grebet af en følelse af fremmedhed og fjendtlighed, der kom oftest i de perioder, hvor grevinde Marja ventede barn. Nu befandt hun sig netop i den tilstand.

»Nå, messieurs et mesdames,« sagde Nikolaj højt og med tilsyneladende munterhed (grevinde Marja syntes, han gjorde det med vilje for at irritere hende), »jeg har været på benene siden klokken seks i morges. I morgen skal jeg lide, så i dag vil jeg hvile mig.«
Og uden et ord til sin kone gik han ind i den lille dagligstue og lagde sig på sofaen.

»Det er altid sådan,« tænkte grevinde Marja. »Han taler med alle undtagen mig. Jeg kan se... jeg kan se, at jeg er frastødende for ham, især når jeg er i denne tilstand.« Hun så ned på sin udvidede figur og i spejlet på sit blege, gullige, afmagrede ansigt, hvori øjnene nu syntes større end ellers.
Og alt irriterede hende — Denisovs råben og latter, Natasjas snak og især et hurtigt blik, Sonja sendte hende.
Sonja var altid den første undskyldning, grevinde Marja fandt for at føle sig irriteret.
Efter at have siddet lidt hos gæsterne uden at forstå noget af det, de sagde, forlod hun stille stuen og gik op i børneværelset.

Børnene legede »rejse til Moskva« i en vogn lavet af stole og inviterede hende med. Hun satte sig ned og legede lidt med dem, men tanken om sin mand og hans grundløse irritation bekymrede hende. Hun rejste sig og gik med besvær på tåspidserne ind i den lille dagligstue.
»Måske sover han ikke; så kan jeg tale med ham,« sagde hun til sig selv. Lille Andrej (hendes ældste søn) fulgte hende på tåspidserne og efterlignede sin mor. Hun lagde ikke mærke til ham.
»Marja, kære, han sover vist — han var så træt,« sagde Sonja, der mødte hende i den store dagligstue (grevinde Marja syntes, at hun krydsede hendes vej overalt). »Andrej kan vække ham.«

Grevinde Marja så sig om, opdagede lille Andrej, der fulgte hende, følte at Sonja havde ret og blev netop derfor rød og havde åbenbart svært ved at lade være med at sige noget skarpt. Hun svarede intet, men for at undgå at adlyde Sonja vinkede hun ad Andrej, at han stille skulle følge hende, og gik hen til døren. Sonja gik ud ad en anden dør. Fra det værelse, hvor Nikolaj sov, hørte grevinde Marja hans jævne åndedrag, hvert eneste drag velkendt for hende. Mens hun lyttede til det, så hun for sig hans glatte, smukke pande, hans overskæg og hele hans ansigt, som hun havde betragtet så ofte i nattens stilhed, mens han sov. Pludselig rørte Nikolaj på sig og rømmede sig. Og i det samme råbte lille Andrej ude foran døren: »Papa! Mama står herude!« Grevinde Marja blegnede af forskrækkelse og gjorde tegn til drengen. Han tav. Et øjeblik var der stille, en stilhed, som var frygtelig for grevinde Marja. Hun vidste, hvor Nikolaj hadede at blive vækket. Så hørte hun ham gennem døren rømme sig igen og røre på sig, og hans stemme sagde gnavent:
»Kan man ikke få et øjebliks fred... Marja, er det dig? Hvorfor bragte du ham herhen?«
»Jeg kom bare for at se ind og lagde ikke mærke til... tilgiv mig...«

Nikolaj hostede og sagde ikke mere. Grevinde Marja gik væk fra døren og fulgte drengen tilbage til børneværelset. Fem minutter efter listede den lille sortøjede Natasja på tre år, sin fars yndling, hen til ham uden at blive set af sin mor. Hendes bror havde fortalt hende, at papa sov, og mama var i dagligstuen. Den lille mørkøjede pige skubbede modigt den knirkende dør op og gik med raske skridt på sine små, solide ben hen til sofaen. Hun så nøje efter, hvordan far lå. Han sov med ryggen til. Så rejste hun sig på tæer og kyssede den hånd, han havde under hovedet. Nikolaj vendte sig med et ømt smil.
»Natasja, Natasja!« lød grevinde Marjas forskræmte hvisken fra døren. »Papa vil sove.«
»Nej, Mama, det vil han ikke,« sagde lille Natasja med overbevisning. »Han griner.«
Nikolaj sænkede benene, rejste sig og tog sin datter i armene.
»Kom ind, Marja,« sagde han til sin kone.
Hun gik ind og satte sig ved sin mand.
»Jeg lagde ikke mærke til, at han fulgte efter mig,« sagde hun frygtsomt. »Jeg kiggede bare ind.«
Nikolaj holdt sin lille pige med den ene arm, så på sin kone, og da han opdagede hendes skyldbevidste udtryk, lagde han den anden arm om hende og kyssede hendes hår.
»Må jeg kysse Mama?« spurgte han Natasja.
Natasja smilede genert.
»Igen!« befalede hun og pegede med en myndig gestus på det sted, hvor Nikolaj havde sat kysset.
»Jeg ved ikke, hvorfor du tror, jeg er vred,« sagde Nikolaj som svar på det spørgsmål, han vidste lå i sin kones sind.
»Du aner ikke, hvor ulykkelig og ensom jeg føler mig, når du er sådan. Det synes mig altid...«
»Marja, lad være med det vrøvl. Du burde skamme dig!« sagde han muntert.
»Det synes mig, at du ikke kan elske mig, at jeg er så hæslig... altid... og nu... i denne tilsta...«

»Åh, hvor er du tåbelig! Det er ikke skønhed, der gør elsket, det er kærlighed, der får os til at se skønhed. Det er kun Malvinaer og kvinder af den slags, der elskes for deres skønhed. Men elsker jeg min kone? Jeg elsker hende ikke, men... jeg ved ikke, hvordan jeg skal udtrykke det. Uden dig, eller når noget sådan her kommer imellem os, kan jeg ikke leve. Kan jeg kysse min finger og elske den? Nej. Men du er ikke min finger, du er mit hele jeg. Nej, det forstår du ikke...«
»Jeg er ikke selv sådan, men jeg forstår godt. Så du er ikke vred på mig?«
»Rasende vred!« sagde han smilende og rejste sig. Og idet han glattede sit hår, begyndte han at gå op og ned i stuen.
»Ved du, hvad jeg har tænkt på, Marja?« begyndte han og tænkte straks højt i sin kones nærværelse, nu da de var blevet forsonet.

Han spurgte ikke, om hun var parat til at lytte. Han var ligeglad. En tanke var opstået hos ham, og den tilhørte hende også. Og han fortalte hende om sin plan om at overtale Pierre til at blive hos dem til foråret.
Grevinde Marja lyttede, til han var færdig, kom med en bemærkning, og begyndte så selv at tænke højt. Hendes tanker handlede om børnene.

»Man kan allerede se kvinden i hende,« sagde hun på fransk og pegede på lille Natasja. »Du bebrejder os kvinder vores mangel på logik. Her er vores logik. Jeg siger: 'Papa vil sove!' men hun siger: 'Nej, han griner.' Og hun havde ret,« sagde grevinde Marja med et lykkeligt smil.

»Ja, ja.« Og Nikolaj tog sin lille datter i sin stærke hånd, løftede hende højt, satte hende på sin skulder, holdt hende i benene og gik rundt i stuen med hende. Der var et udtryk af ubekymret lykke i både fars og datters ansigter.
»Men du ved godt, at du er uretfærdig. Du holder for meget af den her,« hviskede hans kone på fransk.
»Ja, men hvad skal jeg gøre?... Jeg prøver at lade være med at vise det...«
I det øjeblik hørte de lyden af dørens rulle og skridt i forstuen og entréen, som om nogen var ankommet.
»Nogen er kommet.«
»Jeg er sikker på, at det er Pierre. Jeg går ud og ser,« sagde grevinde Marja og forlod stuen.

I hendes fravær tillod Nikolaj sig at galoppere sin lille datter rundt i stuen. Forpustet tog han det leende barn hurtigt ned fra sin skulder og trykkede hende til sit hjerte. Hans kaprioler mindede ham om dans, og mens han så på barnets runde, lykkelige lille ansigt, tænkte han på, hvordan hun ville blive som ung kvinde, når han som gammel mand ville føre hende op til dans og, som hans afdøde far plejede at synge: »Charming Mimi,« ville synge den gamle dans.

»Det er ham, det er ham, Nikolaj!« sagde grevinde Marja, da hun kom ind igen et par minutter senere. »Nu er vores Natasja vågnet til live. Du skulle have set hendes henrykkelse, og hvor han fik det at høre, fordi han var blevet så længe borte. Nå, kom nu, skynd jer! Det er på tide, I to blev skilt ad,« tilføjede hun med et smil og kiggede på den lille pige, der klyngede sig til sin far.
Nikolaj gik ud med barnet i hånden.
Grevinde Marja blev i dagligstuen.

»Jeg ville aldrig, aldrig have troet, at man kan være så lykkelig,« hviskede hun til sig selv. Et smil lyste op i hendes ansigt, men samtidig sukkede hun, og hendes dybe øjne udtrykte en stille bedrøvelse, som om hun gennem sin lykke følte, at der findes en anden slags lykke, der er uopnåelig i dette liv, og som hun i dette øjeblik mindedes.

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: It was the eve of St. Nicholas Day, December fifth, 1820. That year Natasha and her husband and children had been staying at her brother's since early autumn. Pierre had gone to Petersburg on business "for three weeks," as he said, but had now been away for seven. He was expected back any minute.
Besides the Bezukhov family, Nicholas's old friend the retired General Vasili Dmitrich Denisov was also staying with the Rostovs on this fifth of December.

On the sixth—his name day, when the house would be full of visitors—Nicholas knew he would have to swap his Tatar tunic for a dress coat, put on narrow boots with pointed toes, and drive to the new church he had built, then receive congratulations and offer refreshments and talk about the local elections and the year's harvest. But the day before, he considered himself entitled to spend as he usually did. Before dinnertime Nicholas went over the bailiff's accounts from the Ryazan estate belonging to his wife's nephew, wrote two business letters, and strolled through the granaries, the cattle yard, and the stables. After taking measures against the general drunkenness expected the next day because of the holiday, he came in to dinner without having had a moment alone with his wife all day. He sat down at the long table laid for twenty people, around which the whole household was assembled. This included his mother, Sonya (who lived with them), his wife, their three children, their governess, their tutor, his wife's nephew with his tutor, and several others who always dined at the house.

Countess Mary sat at the other end of the table. When her husband sat down, she could tell from the quick way he grabbed his napkin and pushed aside the glass and wineglass in front of him that he was in a bad mood—as sometimes happened, especially before soup and when he came straight from work to the table. Countess Mary knew this mood well and, when she was in a good mood herself, would wait quietly until he had his first spoonful of soup, and only then begin talking—making him admit he had been in a bad mood for no reason. But today she entirely forgot this observation of hers; she felt hurt that he was cross with her for no reason, and she felt miserable. She asked him where he had been. He told her. She then asked whether all was going well on the estate. His frown deepened at her unnatural tone, and he answered briefly.

"So I'm not mistaken," thought Countess Mary. "But why is he cross with me?" She concluded from his tone that he was annoyed with her and wanted to end the conversation. She knew her remarks sounded forced, but couldn't help asking a few more questions.

Thanks to Denisov the conversation at dinner soon became general and lively, and she stopped talking to her husband. When they rose from the table and went as usual to thank the old countess, Countess Mary held out her hand and kissed her husband, asking him why he was angry with her.
"You always have such odd ideas! I didn't even think of being angry," he replied.
But the word "always" seemed to her to mean: "Yes, I am angry, but I won't tell you why."

Nicholas and his wife lived together so happily that even Sonya and the old countess—who felt jealous and would have liked them to disagree—could find nothing to criticize. But they too had their moments of tension. Occasionally, especially right after their happiest periods, a feeling of estrangement and hostility would come over them. This feeling occurred most often when Countess Mary was pregnant. She was pregnant now.

"Well, ladies and gentlemen," Nicholas said loudly and with forced cheerfulness—or so it seemed to Countess Mary, who felt he did it on purpose to annoy her—"I've been on my feet since six this morning. Tomorrow I'll have to suffer through the celebrations, so today I'm going to rest." And without a word to his wife, he went into the little sitting room and lay down on the sofa.
And without a word to his wife he went to the little sitting room and lay down on the sofa.

"That's always the way," thought Countess Mary. "He talks to everyone except me. I can see... I can see that I repel him, especially in this condition." She looked down at her pregnant figure and into the mirror at her pale, sallow, emaciated face with its larger-looking eyes.
And everything irritated her—Denisov's loud voice and laughter, Natasha's chatter, and especially the quick glance Sonya gave her.
Sonya was always the first excuse Countess Mary found for feeling irritated.
Having sat with the visitors for a while without following a word of what they said, she quietly left the room and went to the nursery.

The children were playing "going to Moscow" in a carriage made of chairs and invited her to join them. She sat down and played with them for a little while, but the thought of her husband and his unreasonable ill temper kept nagging at her. She got up and walked on tiptoe, with difficulty, to the small sitting room.
"Maybe he's not asleep. I'll have it out with him," she told herself. Little Andrew, her eldest boy, was following her on tiptoe, imitating his mother. She didn't notice him.
"Mary, dear, I think he's asleep—he was so tired," said Sonya, meeting her in the large sitting room. (It seemed to Countess Mary that Sonya crossed her path everywhere.) "Andrew might wake him."

Countess Mary looked around, saw little Andrew following her, felt that Sonya was right, and for that very reason flushed and with obvious difficulty kept herself from saying something sharp. She said nothing, but—to avoid obeying Sonya—beckoned Andrew to follow her quietly, and went to the door. Sonya went out by the other door. From the room where Nicholas lay asleep, his wife could hear his even breathing, every note of which was familiar to her. As she listened, she could see his smooth, handsome forehead and mustache, and the whole face she had studied so often in the silence of the night when he slept. Nicholas suddenly stirred and cleared his throat. And at that moment, little Andrew shouted from outside the door: "Papa! Mama's standing here!" Countess Mary paled with fright and began signaling to the boy. He fell silent, and for a moment there was a terrible stillness that lasted about a minute. She knew how much Nicholas disliked being woken. Then behind the door she heard another throat-clearing and a movement, and his displeased voice said:
"I can't get a moment's peace... Mary, is that you? Why did you bring him here?"
"I only came to look and didn't notice... I'm sorry..."

Nicholas coughed and said no more. Countess Mary moved away from the door and took the boy back to the nursery. Five minutes later, little black-eyed three-year-old Natasha—her father's pet—having learned from her brother that Papa was asleep and Mama was in the sitting room, ran to her father unnoticed by her mother. The dark-eyed little girl boldly pushed open the creaking door, marched to the sofa with determined little steps, and—seeing that her father was asleep with his back to her—stood on tiptoe and kissed the hand he was resting his head on. Nicholas turned around with a tender smile on his face.
"Natasha, Natasha!" came Countess Mary's frightened whisper from the door. "Papa wants to sleep."
"No, Mama, he doesn't want to sleep," said little Natasha with conviction. "He's laughing."
Nicholas swung his legs down, sat up, and took his daughter in his arms.
"Come in, Mary," he said to his wife.
She came in and sat down beside her husband.
"I didn't notice him following me," she said timidly. "I just looked in."
Holding his little girl with one arm, Nicholas glanced at his wife, and seeing her guilty expression, put his other arm around her and kissed her hair.
"May I kiss Mama?" he asked Natasha.
Natasha smiled shyly.
"Again!" she commanded with a bossy gesture, pointing to the spot where Nicholas had placed the kiss.
"I don't know why you think I'm cross," said Nicholas, answering the question he knew was in his wife's mind.
"You have no idea how unhappy, how lonely I feel when you're like that. It always seems to me—"
"Mary, don't be silly. You should be ashamed of yourself!" he said cheerfully.
"It seems to me that you can't love me, that I'm so plain... always... and now... in this state—"

"Oh, how ridiculous you are! It's not beauty that makes us love—it's love that makes us see beauty. It's only the Malvinas of the world who are loved for their looks. Do I love my wife? I don't just love her—but... I don't know how to put it. Without you, or when something comes between us like today, I feel completely lost—I can't do anything. Do I love my finger? No, but just try cutting it off..."
"I'm not like that myself, but I understand. So you're not angry with me?"
"Terribly angry!" he said, smiling. And he stood up, smoothed his hair, and began pacing the room.
"Do you know, Mary, what I've been thinking?" he began, immediately thinking aloud in his wife's presence now that they had made up.
He didn't ask if she was ready to listen. He didn't care. A thought had occurred to him and so it belonged to her too. And he told her his plan to convince Pierre to stay with them until spring.
Countess Mary listened until he had finished, made a comment, and in turn began thinking aloud. Her thoughts were about the children.

"You can already see the woman in her," she said in French, pointing to little Natasha. "You men accuse us women of being illogical. Here's our logic. I say: 'Papa wants to sleep!' but she says, 'No, he's laughing.' And she was right," said Countess Mary with a happy smile.

"Yes, yes." And Nicholas, taking his little daughter in his strong hand, lifted her high, set her on his shoulder, held her by the legs, and paced the room. Father and daughter wore identical expressions of carefree happiness.
"But you know, you may be unfair. You're too fond of this one," his wife whispered in French.
"Yes, but what can I do?... I try not to show it..."
At that moment they heard the sound of the door-pull and footsteps in the hall and front room, as if someone had arrived.
"Someone's here."
"I'm sure it's Pierre. I'll go and see," said Countess Mary, and she left the room.

In her absence, Nicholas allowed himself to give his little daughter a gallop around the room. Out of breath, he quickly lifted the laughing child from his shoulder and pressed her to his heart. His capering reminded him of dancing, and looking at the child's round, happy little face, he thought of what she would be like when he was an old man, taking her to balls, and he imagined her dancing the mazurka with some lanky young man, just as his late father-in-law had once danced Daniel Cooper with his daughter.

"It's him, it's him, Nicholas!" said Countess Mary, coming back a few minutes later. "Now our Natasha has come to life. You should have seen her face light up, and how she scolded him for staying away so long. Well, come along now, quick, quick! Separate yourselves at last!" she said, smiling as she looked at the little girl pressed against her father.
Nicholas went out, holding the child by the hand.
Countess Mary stayed behind in the sitting room.

"I would never, never have believed anyone could be so happy," she whispered to herself. A smile lit up her face, but at the same time she sighed, and a quiet sadness showed in her deep eyes—as though she felt, through her happiness, that there is another kind of happiness, unattainable in this life, which she could not help thinking of at that moment.
